Urban Farming On New York Skyline

By: Diana Lucas | Delivery

The New York sky line and 900 farrms

Press Release:


A farm in the middle of New York City. No space you say? A group of idealists not only developed the
biggest rooftop farm in the US and probably the world, but managed to turn the initiative into a massive
commercial venture. Carte Blanche meets the entrepreneurial individuals who turned a seemingly
impossible left-field idea into a sky-high success.

Script:


V/O 15 sec
Brooklyn, the largest borough of New York City, lies across the Hudson River from Manhattan ….and its here in Brooklyn’s Naval Yard, Warehouse No 3 that we find something really unexpected…… a farm on a roof

Link
Seven years ago this group of idealists had this crazy idea they arrived here early one winters morning equipped with shovels seedlings and thousands of kilograms of soil

V/O 7 sec
(1.2 million pounds) Over half a million kilogrammes of soil to be exact that needed to be taken eleven stories up to the roof.

Anastasia: We literally craned the soil up bag by bag. The bags were 3 000 pounds each we split them into dirt buggies and cart them across the roof.

V/O 6 sec
Anastasia Cole Plakias a New York city dweller is one of the farms co-founders.

Anastasia nothing like this had ever been done before, there was no road map for us to follow so we really were writing the book and really truly it was a labour of love we had friends, family members anyone we could talk into coming by and helping out.

Devi So how long did it take to cart the soil up?
Anastasia: It took about 6 days of craning soil over the course of about 2 weeks, a lot of digging a lot of raking, a lot of measuring soil depth and then we had ourselves a farm.

V/O 15 sec
This was the beginning of Brooklyn Grange Farm, now covering an area of over two acres, on two warehouse rooftops. The pioneers, a group of small time urban farmers with a mission to build the largest roof top farm in the world.

Anastasia: We were all entrepreneurs who were working on urban agriculture as a hobby but what we realised is at the scale we were practising it which was small gardens here and there it was really nothing more than a really expensive hobby and we felt that in order to see this concept on rooftops all over the world it needed to be sustainable and for that we needed to scale.

Devi: Did people say you were nuts?
Anastasia: We got a little bit of you’re nuts, we got a lot of support we got a tremendous amount of support. …. ///

V/O 10 sec
Creating a farm this size on a rooftop, meant there were a lot of challenges, one of the biggest was isolating buildings that could sustain the weight of the farm.

Anastasia: We looked for buildings that are structurally sound enough to support the weight of our saturated soil meaning our solid fully wet with water and then we designed the green roof itself to drain very well. green roof soil drains quiet well and the green roof system that you put under that soil helps quiet a bit with that transmitability.

Devi: What did you plant first?
Anastasia: I think the first crop that we transplanted into our soil was a tomato seedling, the tomato seedling was ready to spread its roots it had been coped up in a small green house at a friend’s garden because it took us longer than anticipated to find a site for our farm because landlords were a bit trepidatous about entering into this relationship with us when this was truly a concept that nobody had tried before.

Devi Do you sell how does it work?
Anastasia: Yup we sell every last leaf that we grow up here we have to be really mindful of eeking out as much revenue as we can because we are working with such a small space, our number one crop is cut salad greens. We sell the vast majority of our crops and most of our salad greens to whole sale customers, restaurants, small mom and pop grocers what have you. And some of our shoppers walk over to the farm from their apartment shop from us and walk those vegetables back, that’s a process that makes it from seed to plate without ever using any fossil fuels, which in this day and age is truly a rarity.

V/O 19 sec 22 000 kilo or over 20 tons
Brooklyn Grange produces a 50 000 pounds of produce a year, they farm organically but what they are equally passionate about is, creating green spaces in an increasing industrialised and overcrowded city ….it’s not all about commerce.

Anastasia: This is definitely not the most efficient way to farm we don’t have tractors up here but it is a deeply necessary endeavour in NY city in 2017. We find that our urban population is increasingly alienated not just from food and farming but from nature.

Devi: How many urban farms in the US?
Anastasia: I don’t know the number of urban farms in NY some of them are tucked away on balconies, rooftops, backyards out of site it’s a growing number. NYC has a rapidly growing urban farm population which is exciting to see.

V/O 7 sec
One of the original rooftop farms in New York is Eagle Street Rooftop Farm which sits on the top of a film stage in Brooklyn.

Devi How big is this movement?
Warren: Its growing massively its exploding This was the first in Brooklyn and from this others have been bred from impactful wonderful.

V/O 8 sec
It was Annie Novak who started this farm back in 2009, she’s made it her life’s work to educate children about where food comes from…

Warren: Annie is really like the most sincere wonderful amazing person who really puts her energy love and passion into everything.

Warren: There’s amazing classes from local schools teaching them how to grow especially in the city growing up in an apartment in NYC you don’t necessarily have the knowledge and wherewithal.to have students come to this amazing roof top … it’s educational and great for the whole community

V/O 13 sec
Brooklyn Grange farm’s success has snowballed, the rooftop holds weddings, fashion shoots dinner parties and educational tours. To date they’ve hosted 17 000 young New Yorkers.

Anastasia We began receiving so many requests from school group organisations who wanted to bring their students here and so we started city growers our sister organisation 501 C3 Non profit that brings kids up to learn about food and farming developing environmental literacy something that’s sorely lacking in today’s youth.

Devi: Did you think there would be this successful?
Anastasia: don’t know if we were prepared for quiet this level of interest I am a native New Yorker born and raised here, I felt the need keenly.
Devi: So are you breaking even making small profits?
Anastasia We have been profitable since 2012, when we began paying our investors distributions.

V/O 10 sec
Their core belief is about growing nutritious food in the city they live in …their passion and commitment is the very reason for their success.

Anastasia: We have had a tremendous amount of international interest. We have spoken at universities and colleges South America, Europe Asia, Middle East and were currently consulting on projects in Paris and Bangkok

Devi: As far afield as Bangkok?
Anastasia: Absolutely and that’s not the end for us we are looking at the globe, we are looking at creative ways of greening cities all around the world. We are currently working on expansion into a third site in Brooklyn, so we want to have a local impact on our own community but we also want to have a global impact

Devi: I have never been to a farm like this in my life before and certainly not with this view.
Anastasia: So many things are unexpected on our farm this confluence of crickets and construction noises. The birds and the sirens. This farm is truly an exercise in unexpected combinations Its not something you see every day but it also asks our visitors to think about what possibilities there are for cities for farmland that’s really what we want for every one who comes to the farm to think what else might be possible.
